SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks a plant with no big, bright flowers (maize, grass, kale, mango) does not flower.

example.question: Is a maize plant a flowering plant or a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Non-flowering plant
example.correct_answer: Flowering plant

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child counts only showy petals as flowers. The flowers of maize (the tassel and the silk), grasses and many trees are small and green or yellow.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Use crops and grasses, never roses or hibiscus, and offer the answer "non-flowering".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Look closely at a maize tassel and a young cob with the class and call both flowers. Anything that makes seeds inside a fruit or grain belongs to the flowering plants.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Many flowers are small and not bright. Maize has flowers too: the tassel at the top and the silk on the cob. A plant that makes seeds inside fruits or grains is a flowering plant.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: Plant-concept research reports that children restrict 'flower' to showy flowers (Bell and Barker 1982; Tunnicliffe and Reiss 1999). Cited from memory: verify the references.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks every tree is a flowering plant, including cypress and pine, which make cones.

example.question: Is a cypress tree a flowering or a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Flowering plant
example.correct_answer: Non-flowering plant

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child sorts by size or by being a plant with seeds, and has not met cones as a different way of making seeds.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Offer cypress or pine next to mango and ask for flowering or non-flowering.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Show a cypress cone. Cones hold seeds but they are not flowers and there is no fruit. Compare with a mango flower and fruit.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Cypress and pine are trees, but they make cones, not flowers and fruits. That makes them non-flowering plants.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks every plant has flowers, so ferns and mosses must flower too.

example.question: Does a fern make flowers?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, but very small ones
example.correct_answer: No

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child assumes all green plants flower, because the plants at home and at school all do.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask about ferns or mosses and offer "yes, hidden flowers".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Look at the underside of a fern frond for the spore cases, and at moss capsules. These plants never make flowers.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Ferns and mosses never make flowers. They make tiny spores instead. They are non-flowering plants.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Decides by what the plant looks like today: a bean or kale plant with no flower this week is "non-flowering".

example.question: A kale plant in a shamba has no flowers this week. Is kale a non-flowering plant?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has no flowers now
example.correct_answer: No, kale makes flowers when it is left to grow

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child classifies by the moment of looking, not by what the plant can do over its whole life.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Describe a flowering plant that has not flowered yet, such as a bean seedling or kale cut every week.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Follow one bean plant through weeks: seedling, flower, pod. A plant is flowering if it makes flowers at some time in its life.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Look at the whole life of the plant. Kale and beans make flowers when they are old enough, even if you do not see any today. They are flowering plants.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge: children judge living-thing and plant status by what is visible at the time. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Mixes up petals and sepals, calling the small green parts below the flower the petals.

example.question: Which part is the small green leaf-like part at the base of a flower?
example.wrong_answer: Petal
example.correct_answer: Sepal

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child names the part by the word they know best (petal) and has not looked at the green ring under the coloured petals.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Describe the green part by position and colour and offer petal as a distractor.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Take a bean or hibiscus flower apart. Petals are coloured and on the inside. Sepals are green and underneath, and they covered the bud.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Petals are the coloured parts. The green parts at the bottom that covered the flower when it was a bud are the sepals.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Swaps the stamen and the pistil.

example.question: Which part of a flower is the stamen?
example.wrong_answer: The part in the middle with the ovary at its base
example.correct_answer: The part with a thin stalk and a small pollen-holding top

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The words sound alike and both stand in the middle of the flower.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask for the part with pollen, and offer the pistil.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Say the rhyme: STamen has the pollen (Sticks up with an anther), PIStil has the Pip (seed) place. Draw both from a real flower.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: The stamens are the thin stalks that carry the pollen on top. The pistil is the part in the middle that has the ovary at its base.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks the stigma is the top of the stamen, or that the anther is part of the pistil.

example.question: Which part of a flower is sticky and catches pollen?
example.wrong_answer: Anther
example.correct_answer: Stigma

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child knows both are small knobs at the top of a thin part and mixes them up.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask which part holds pollen and which part catches pollen, with both names as options.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Pollen is made on the anther (A for "at the stamen") and lands on the sticky stigma (S for "sticky").
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: The anther is the top of the stamen and holds the pollen. The stigma is the sticky top of the pistil, where pollen lands.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Gives the sepals the job of attracting insects and the petals the job of protecting the bud.

example.question: Which part of a flower protects the bud before it opens?
example.wrong_answer: Petals
example.correct_answer: Sepals

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child has swapped the two names or has assumed the bigger, brighter part does the protecting.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask for the protecting part and offer petals first.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Show a bud: the green sepals wrap it. Then show an open flower: the bright petals are the sign for insects.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Sepals are the tough green parts that wrap the bud. Petals are bright to attract insects and birds.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks pollen is a seed, or that the stamen makes the seeds.

example.question: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
example.wrong_answer: Ovary
example.correct_answer: Anther

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child links a flower with seeds and has not separated pollen (made on the anther) from seeds (made in the ovary after pollen arrives).
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask what the stamen makes and offer "seeds".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Rub an anther on paper to see the yellow pollen. Then cut open a young bean pod: the seeds grow in the ovary. They are different things.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Pollen is a fine dust made on the anther. Seeds grow later inside the ovary. Pollen is not a seed.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Gives the ovary the job of making pollen, or gives the anther the job of holding the seeds.

example.question: Which part of a flower holds the ovules that later become seeds?
example.wrong_answer: Anther
example.correct_answer: Ovary

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child knows the flower makes both pollen and seeds but has not tied each to its own part.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Offer the anther as the part that holds ovules.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Make a two-column chart: anther - makes pollen; ovary - holds ovules, later the seeds.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: The ovary is at the base of the pistil and holds the ovules that become seeds. The anther makes pollen.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks fruits grow straight from the stem or roots, not from the flower.

example.question: From which part of a pumpkin plant does the pumpkin fruit grow?
example.wrong_answer: The root
example.correct_answer: The flower (its ovary)

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child sees fruit hanging from the plant and has never watched the flower wither and the fruit swell in its place.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask where a fruit comes from and offer root or stem.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Watch a tomato or pumpkin flower for two weeks: the petals drop and the base of the flower swells into the fruit.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Look at what grows where the flower was. The petals fall off and the ovary at the base swells to become the fruit.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: Children often do not link fruits with flowers (Driver et al. 1994 on plant reproduction). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Mixes up pollination (carrying pollen to a stigma) with carrying seeds away to new places.

example.question: A bee moves from one pumpkin flower to another with yellow dust on its legs. What is happening?
example.wrong_answer: Seeds are being carried to a new place
example.correct_answer: Pollen is being carried to a stigma

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child knows animals and wind help plants spread and uses one idea for both jobs.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Describe pollen movement and offer seed dispersal.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Two charts: pollination is before the seed (pollen to stigma). Dispersal is after (seed to new ground).
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Pollination is carrying pollen from an anther to a stigma. Carrying seeds away to new places is another job, called seed dispersal.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks flowers make fruits whether or not pollen ever reaches them, so bees and the wind do not matter.

example.question: A farmer sprays a pesticide that kills all the bees near his pumpkin flowers. What is likely to happen to the pumpkins?
example.wrong_answer: They will still grow just as many fruits
example.correct_answer: Fewer fruits will grow

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child thinks the plant fills the fruit on its own and does not link pollen arriving with seeds starting to grow.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Give a scenario with no pollinators and offer "no change".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Compare a flower covered with a net bag (no visitors) and an open one over two weeks.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Many flowers, such as pumpkin and passion fruit, need pollen to be carried to them. With no bees, fewer flowers are pollinated and fewer fruits grow.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks flowers are only for decoration and smell.

example.question: Why are flowers important in nature, apart from looking beautiful?
example.wrong_answer: They are only there to look and smell nice
example.correct_answer: They make fruits and seeds and feed bees and other insects

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child knows flowers from bouquets and gardens and has not thought about what they do for the plant.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask for the importance of flowers and offer "to look nice" as an answer.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: List everything on the lunch plate that began as a flower: maize, beans, mango, tomato.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Flowers are much more than decoration. They make the fruits and seeds we eat, they feed bees, and they bring in money for farmers.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Thinks insects on flowers harm the plant and should be killed.

example.question: Bees visit the flowers on Wanjiru's bean plants. What should she think about the bees?
example.wrong_answer: They help the plant make seeds, so she should leave them
example.correct_answer: They are harming the plant, so she should kill them

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child knows some insects eat crops and lumps all insects together.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Offer "kill the insects" as a distractor.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Show a bee carrying pollen. Separate insects that eat leaves from those that carry pollen.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, so the plant can make seeds. They help, and they also give us honey.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..error: Does not link everyday foods (mango, beans, tomato, maize grain) with flowers.

example.question: Which food came from a flower?
example.wrong_answer: Cassava roots
example.correct_answer: Mangoes

SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..cause: The child thinks of flowers as separate from food plants.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..reveals: Ask which food came from a flower and offer a root.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..help: Trace a mango back to the mango flower in a season of the year.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..feedback: Fruits and grains grow from flowers. Mangoes, beans, tomatoes and maize all started as flowers.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.CLASSIFICATION_OF_PLANTS..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.error: Thinks big animals are vertebrates and small animals are not (or the other way round).

example.question: Is a small mouse a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: Invertebrate, because it is small
example.correct_answer: Vertebrate, because it has a backbone

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.cause: The child uses size, which is easy to see, in place of the backbone, which is hidden.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.reveals: Use a very small vertebrate (mouse, gecko) and a big invertebrate (crab, octopus).
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.help: Feel your own backbone, then compare with the thin skeleton of a small fish.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.feedback: Size does not matter. A mouse is small but it has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge: children classify animals by obvious features such as size. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.error: Thinks an animal with no legs (snake, fish) cannot be a vertebrate.

example.question: A snake has no legs. Is a snake a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: No, because it has no legs
example.correct_answer: Yes, because it has a backbone

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.cause: The child links "animal with bones" with legs to stand on.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.reveals: Use a snake or a fish and offer legs as the reason.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.help: Look at a snake skeleton picture: a long backbone with many bones.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.feedback: Legs are not needed. A snake has a long backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.error: Thinks a hard shell or hard outside (crab, beetle, snail) means the animal has a backbone.

example.question: A crab has a hard shell. Is a crab a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because its shell is hard like a bone
example.correct_answer: No, because it has no backbone

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.cause: The child has seen hard parts on the animal and takes them for bones.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.reveals: Use crab, beetle or snail with "hard shell" as the offered reason.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.help: Compare the inside skeleton of a fish with the outside shell of a crab.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.feedback: A crab has a hard shell on the outside, but no backbone inside. It is an invertebrate.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_CH.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.error: Thinks a bat is a bird because it flies.

example.question: To which group does a bat belong?
example.wrong_answer: Birds
example.correct_answer: Mammals

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.cause: The child groups by how the animal moves, not by body covering and how the young are fed.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.reveals: Offer the bat with birds in the options.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.help: A bat has fur and feeds its young on milk. No feathers. Birds have feathers and lay eggs.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.feedback: Flying does not make a bird. A bat has fur and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.source: Children group animals by where they live or how they move (Braund 1991; Kattmann 2001). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.error: Thinks any animal that lives in water is a fish (dolphin, crocodile, hippo, frog).

example.question: To which group does a dolphin belong?
example.wrong_answer: Fish
example.correct_answer: Mammals

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.cause: The child groups by habitat, not by body features.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.reveals: Offer dolphin or crocodile with fish in the options.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.help: Fish have gills and scales. A dolphin breathes air with lungs and feeds its young on milk.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.feedback: Living in water does not make a fish. A dolphin breathes air and feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.source: Braund 1991; Kattmann 2001: habitat-based grouping. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.error: Mixes up reptiles and amphibians (thinking chameleons and lizards are amphibians, or frogs are reptiles).

example.question: To which group does a chameleon belong?
example.wrong_answer: Amphibians
example.correct_answer: Reptiles

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.cause: The child knows both groups are cold to the touch and lay eggs and has not looked at the skin.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.reveals: Offer chameleon or frog with the other group.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.help: Reptiles have dry scales and lay eggs on land. Amphibians have moist skin and start life in water.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.feedback: A chameleon has dry scales and lays its eggs on land. That makes it a reptile.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.error: Thinks a bird that cannot fly (an ostrich) is not a bird.

example.question: To which group does an ostrich belong?
example.wrong_answer: Mammals, because it cannot fly
example.correct_answer: Birds

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.cause: The child uses flying to define a bird, not feathers and eggs with hard shells.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.help: List what an ostrich has: feathers, wings, a beak, hard-shelled eggs.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.feedback: An ostrich cannot fly, but it has feathers, wings and a beak, and it lays eggs. It is a bird.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.source: Braund 1991: a bird must fly. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.error: Thinks any animal that lays eggs is a bird.

example.question: A crocodile lays eggs. Is it a bird?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because birds lay eggs
example.correct_answer: No, it is a reptile

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.cause: The child has learned that birds lay eggs and does not know that other groups do too.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.reveals: Use crocodile, tortoise or tilapia with the reason "lays eggs".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.help: Make a chart of which groups lay eggs: birds, reptiles, fish, amphibians.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.feedback: Birds lay eggs, but so do reptiles, fish and amphibians. A crocodile has dry scales, so it is a reptile.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_GR.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.error: Thinks only fish have scales, so snakes and crocodiles do not.

example.question: Which group of vertebrates has dry scales and lays eggs on land?
example.wrong_answer: Fish
example.correct_answer: Reptiles

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.cause: The child links scales with fish because fish scales are the ones seen at the market.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.reveals: Ask for the group with dry scales and offer fish.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.help: Look at a snake skin or a chameleon and feel the dry scales. Compare with wet fish scales.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.feedback: Fish have wet scales and live in water. Reptiles such as snakes and crocodiles have dry scales and lay their eggs on land.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.error: Thinks any animal with wings is a bird.

example.question: Which feature do all birds have, and no other group of vertebrates?
example.wrong_answer: Wings
example.correct_answer: Feathers

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.cause: The child uses wings, the most noticeable feature, and forgets that bats and insects have wings too.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.reveals: Ask for the feature found only in birds and offer wings.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.help: List flying animals: a bat has wings but fur; a butterfly has wings but no backbone. Only birds have feathers.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.feedback: Bats and insects have wings, but only birds have feathers. Feathers are found in birds and no other group.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.error: Thinks amphibians live only in water, or that the word means "lives in water".

example.question: What does it mean when we say a frog is an amphibian?
example.wrong_answer: It lives only in water
example.correct_answer: It spends part of its life in water and part on land

SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.cause: The child connects frogs with ponds and does not know the young live in water and adults can live on land.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.reveals: Ask the meaning of amphibian and offer "lives only in water".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.help: Follow the life of a frog: eggs and tadpole in water, adult hops on land.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.feedback: Amphibians live part of their life in water and part on land. Tadpoles live in water; adult frogs can live on land.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.VERTEBRATES.VERTEBRATE_FE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks air goes down the same pipe as food, or mixes the windpipe with the food pipe.

example.question: Which pipe carries air from the nose to the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: The food pipe (gullet)
example.correct_answer: The windpipe (trachea)

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child knows there is one pipe down the neck and does not know there are two.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Offer the food pipe as a distractor.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Feel the ridged windpipe at the front of the neck. The food pipe is behind it and goes to the stomach.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: There are two pipes in the neck. The windpipe, or trachea, carries air to the lungs. The food pipe carries food to the stomach.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Does not know where the diaphragm is (puts it in the neck, or thinks it is part of the lungs).

example.question: Which part of the breathing system is the sheet of muscle under the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: The trachea
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The word is new and is not seen or felt from outside.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Describe the diaphragm by position and offer the other names.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Draw the body with the diaphragm as a dome under the lungs. Feel your belly rise and fall as you breathe.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under the lungs. It is the part that moves when you breathe.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the lungs are low in the belly, or that there is just one.

example.question: Where are the lungs?
example.wrong_answer: In the belly, next to the stomach
example.correct_answer: In the chest, inside the ribs

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: Children draw the body from outside and place the lungs low or in the middle (Mintzes 1984 reports young children's body-organ drawings).
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask for the position of the lungs and offer the belly.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Put hands on the upper chest and feel the ribs moving. The lungs are behind them.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: There are two lungs, high in the chest and protected by the ribs. The stomach is lower, in the belly.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: Mintzes (1984), Naive theories in biology: children's concepts of the human body, School Science and Mathematics. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the air we breathe goes to the stomach.

example.question: Where does the air go after the windpipe?
example.wrong_answer: To the stomach
example.correct_answer: To the lungs

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child has not separated the two pipes and the idea that "air goes down" ends in the belly.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask where air goes after the trachea and offer the stomach.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Breathe in with the hands on the chest, then on the belly: the chest and the diaphragm move, the stomach does not take in the air.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Air goes to the lungs, not to the stomach. The stomach is for food. Your belly only moves because the diaphragm moves.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: Mann and Treagust (1998), pencil-and-paper instrument on breathing, gas exchange and respiration, Australian Science Teachers Journal. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the lungs have muscles and fill and empty themselves like balloons.

example.question: What helps the lungs fill with air when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: The lungs pull the air in by themselves
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child treats the lungs as the only moving part, like a balloon that inflates itself.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what makes air come in and offer the lungs themselves.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Use a bottle with a balloon inside and a balloon sheet at the bottom to model the diaphragm.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: The lungs have no muscles. The diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs move, and that makes the lungs fill and empty.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks we breathe in only oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.

example.question: Which statement about the air we breathe out is true?
example.wrong_answer: It has no oxygen in it at all
example.correct_answer: It still has some oxygen, and more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child has heard "oxygen in, carbon dioxide out" and takes it as the whole story.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what is in breathed-out air and offer "no oxygen".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Remind the class that mouth-to-mouth breathing works because breathed-out air has oxygen left.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Breathed-out air has less oxygen than the air we breathe in, but it still has some. It also has more carbon dioxide.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: Mann and Treagust (1998). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the nose is only for smelling.

example.question: Besides smelling, what do the hairs and mucus in the nose do?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, the nose is only for smelling
example.correct_answer: They trap dust and germs from the air we breathe in

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child knows the nose as a sense organ and not as a part of the breathing system.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what else the nose does and offer "nothing".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Look at a tissue after a dusty day: the dust has been trapped in the nose.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: The nose also cleans and warms the air. The hairs and sticky mucus trap dust and germs before the air reaches the lungs.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the chest gets smaller or the ribs move in when we breathe in.

example.question: What happens to the chest when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: It gets smaller as the ribs move in
example.correct_answer: It gets bigger as the ribs move up and out

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child thinks of "squeezing" the air in, not of making space for it.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what the chest does when breathing in and offer "it gets smaller".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Put both hands on the ribs and take a deep breath: feel them move out and up.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: When you breathe in, the ribs move up and out and the diaphragm moves down. The chest gets bigger and air comes in.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks the air fills the chest and pushes the ribs out, so the air does the work.

example.question: What is the first thing that happens when you breathe in?
example.wrong_answer: Air rushes in and pushes the chest out
example.correct_answer: The diaphragm and rib muscles move and the chest gets bigger

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child reverses cause and effect: air arrives first, the chest follows.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what comes first and offer "air comes in".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Use a bell-jar model: pulling the rubber sheet down makes the balloon fill. The air follows the space.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: The muscles move first. The chest gets bigger, and then air flows in to fill the space. The air does not push the chest out.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: Mann and Treagust (1998). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks asthma can be caught from another person.

example.question: Can a child catch asthma from a classmate who has it?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it spreads like a cold
example.correct_answer: No, asthma does not spread from person to person

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child treats every illness of the chest or throat as catching.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask whether asthma spreads and offer "yes".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Compare asthma (airways narrow, not an infection) with a cold (a virus that spreads).
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Asthma is not an infection. A child with asthma cannot pass it on. Dust, smoke or cold air can start an asthma attack.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks sneezing and itchy eyes from dust or pollen are a cold caught from someone.

example.question: Wambui sneezes and has itchy eyes every time she sweeps the dusty classroom. What is the most likely cause?
example.wrong_answer: She has caught a cold from another child
example.correct_answer: She has an allergy to the dust

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child links sneezing with colds only.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Give the sneezing story with dust and offer "caught a cold".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Ask when the sneezing starts and stops: if it begins with dust and ends when the dust is gone, it points to an allergy.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Sneezing that starts with dust or pollen and stops without it is an allergy, not a cold. An allergy cannot be caught from another person.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks all coughs and colds are the same illness with the same cause.

example.question: Which of these can spread from one person to another?
example.wrong_answer: Asthma
example.correct_answer: A common cold

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child treats every breathing problem as "a cough".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask which can spread and put asthma or allergy next to the cold.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: List causes: cold and COVID-19 by viruses, asthma and allergy by sensitive airways.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Colds and COVID-19 are caused by viruses and spread between people. Asthma and allergy do not spread.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks a cold is caused by cold weather, rain or a cold drink.

example.question: What causes a common cold?
example.wrong_answer: Cold weather and getting wet in the rain
example.correct_answer: A virus that spreads from one person to another

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: Colds are more common in the cold season and the child links the two as cause and effect.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask for the cause of a cold and offer cold weather.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Show how the cold spreads when someone coughs without covering. Weather can help the virus spread but does not cause it.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: A cold is caused by a virus that spreads from person to person. Cold weather does not cause it.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge (children's ideas about illness and germs). Cited from memory; to confirm by a teacher.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks medicine called antibiotics cures a cold or COVID-19.

example.question: Juma has a cold. What helps him get better?
example.wrong_answer: Taking antibiotics, which kill the cold virus
example.correct_answer: Rest and drinking water; antibiotics do not kill viruses

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child has heard that clinics give medicine for coughs and thinks one medicine fits all illnesses.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask what cures a cold and offer antibiotics.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Separate viruses (colds, COVID-19) from bacteria (some chest infections). Only a health worker decides on medicine.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Antibiotics do not kill viruses, and a cold is caused by a virus. Rest and water help. Go to a clinic if the cough is bad or does not go away.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher or health worker before use with children.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks washing hands does not matter for illnesses of the breathing system.

example.question: Why does washing hands help to stop a cold spreading?
example.wrong_answer: It does not help, because colds are only in the nose
example.correct_answer: Germs on the hands can reach the nose and mouth

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: The child connects handwashing with stomach illnesses only.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask why wash hands to stop a cold and offer "it does not help".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Show glitter on the hands to see how it reaches the face.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Hands pick up virus from surfaces and then touch the nose, eyes and mouth. Washing them helps to stop it.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..error: Thinks smoke from a cooking fire in a closed room is harmless.

example.question: Why is it better to cook outdoors or in a kitchen with a chimney?
example.wrong_answer: Smoke does not harm the lungs, so it makes no difference
example.correct_answer: Smoke can harm the lungs and make coughing and asthma worse

SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..cause: Smoke from cooking is part of everyday life and the child has never linked it to illness.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..reveals: Ask about smoke in the kitchen and offer "no difference".
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..help: Ask the class how their eyes and chest feel in a smoky kitchen.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..feedback: Smoke irritates the nose and lungs. It can bring on coughs and asthma. A chimney or an open door lets it out.
SCIE.G5.LIVING.THE_HUMAN_BREATHING_SYST..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..error: Thinks that once substances are mixed they change into something new and cannot be got back.

example.question: Salt is stirred into water and seems to disappear. Can the salt be got back?
example.wrong_answer: No, the salt has gone for ever
example.correct_answer: Yes, the salt is still there and can be got back

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..cause: The child confuses mixing with cooking or burning, where new substances do form.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..reveals: Use dissolving or sand and water and ask whether the parts are still there.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..help: Leave salty water in the sun in a plate. The salt reappears as the water dries.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..feedback: In a mixture each substance stays the same and can be separated again. Salty water dries and leaves the salt behind.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..error: Thinks a mixture must be made on purpose, so air, soil and muddy water are single things.

example.question: Is air a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, air is one substance
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is made of several gases

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..cause: The child links the word mixture with kitchen or classroom mixing.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..reveals: Ask about air or soil and offer "one substance".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..help: Look at soil in water: sand, clay and bits of plants settle in layers.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..feedback: Mixtures can be natural. Air is a mixture of gases, and soil holds sand, clay and bits of plants.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..error: Thinks the parts of a mixture must be in equal amounts.

example.question: Wafula puts one spoon of sand in a bucket of water. Is it a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, the parts are not equal
example.correct_answer: Yes, the parts can be in any amounts

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..cause: The child mixes up mixtures with recipes that need fixed amounts.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..reveals: Use very different amounts and offer "not a mixture".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..help: Make three sand-and-water mixtures of different amounts and compare.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..feedback: The parts of a mixture can be in any amounts. One spoon of sand in a bucket of water is still a mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_MEANING..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.error: Thinks dissolved salt or sugar has disappeared, so salty water is only water, not a mixture.

example.question: Is salt dissolved in water a mixture?
example.wrong_answer: No, the salt has disappeared so it is only water
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is a homogeneous mixture of salt and water

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.cause: The child cannot see the salt, so thinks it is gone.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.reveals: Use a clear salt solution and offer "only water".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.help: Taste the water, or let it dry to show the salt.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.feedback: You cannot see the salt, but it is still there. Salty water is a mixture, and it looks the same all through, so it is homogeneous.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.error: Thinks a clear liquid must be pure, one substance only.

example.question: Sugar is dissolved in clear water. Is the water pure?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is clear
example.correct_answer: No, it is a mixture of sugar and water

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.cause: Clear and clean are used as the same word.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.reveals: Offer "yes, it is clear" as a reason.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.help: Taste the sugar water: clear but sweet.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.feedback: Clear does not mean pure. Sweet or salty water is clear, but it holds sugar or salt too. It is a mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.error: Thinks stirring makes any mixture the same all through (soil in water, oil in water).

example.question: Muddy water is stirred well. Is it homogeneous?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has been stirred it looks the same all through
example.correct_answer: No, the soil settles and different parts can be seen

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.cause: The child sees an even brown for a short time and calls it uniform.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.reveals: Use a freshly stirred sand or soil mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.help: Stir soil in water and leave it for ten minutes. Layers form.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.feedback: Stirred muddy water looks even for a short time, but the soil settles at the bottom. Different parts can be seen, so it is heterogeneous.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.HOMOGENEOUS_OR_H.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.error: Calls salt dissolved in water a liquid-liquid mixture because it looks like liquid.

example.question: Salt is dissolved in water. What type of mixture is this?
example.wrong_answer: Liquid-liquid
example.correct_answer: Solid-liquid

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.cause: The child classifies by how the mixture looks after mixing, not by the states of the parts before.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.reveals: Use dissolving examples and offer liquid-liquid.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.help: Name the state of each part before they were mixed: salt (solid), water (liquid).
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.feedback: Look at the parts before they were mixed. Salt is a solid and water is a liquid, so this is a solid-liquid mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.error: Thinks a thick liquid (cooking oil, honey) is a solid.

example.question: Cooking oil is mixed with water. What type of mixture is this?
example.wrong_answer: Solid-liquid, because oil is thick
example.correct_answer: Liquid-liquid

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.cause: The child equates thick with solid.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.reveals: Use oil, honey or milk and offer solid-liquid.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.help: Pour oil: it flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.feedback: Oil is thick but it flows and takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid. Oil and water make a liquid-liquid mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.MIXTURE_TYPES.M_.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.error: Thinks filtering separates any mixture, including dissolved salt or stones from rice.

example.question: Which method separates stones from rice?
example.wrong_answer: Filtering
example.correct_answer: Picking

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.cause: Filtering is the best-known method and the child uses it for everything.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.reveals: Offer filtering for a dry solid-solid mixture.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.help: Filter paper only works when one part is a liquid with solid bits in it. Try salt water on filter paper and taste the water.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.feedback: Filtering is for solids mixed in a liquid. Stones in rice are both solids, so you pick them out or use a sieve.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.error: Thinks a magnet picks up every metal (aluminium, copper, brass).

example.question: A jua kali worker has iron nails and aluminium bits mixed in a box. What can a magnet pick out?
example.wrong_answer: Both the nails and the aluminium bits
example.correct_answer: Only the iron nails

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.cause: The child has learned "magnets pick up metals" and has not tested different metals.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.reveals: Mix an iron item with aluminium or copper and ask what the magnet takes.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.help: Test an iron nail, an aluminium sufuria piece and a copper wire with a magnet.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.feedback: A magnet picks up iron and steel, not every metal. Aluminium and copper are not picked up.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.source: Common test of children's ideas about magnets (D94). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.error: Thinks a separating funnel separates a solid from a liquid.

example.question: Which mixture is separated with a separating funnel?
example.wrong_answer: Sand and water
example.correct_answer: Cooking oil and water

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.cause: The child knows the funnel is for liquids and does not know it needs two liquids that do not mix.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.reveals: Offer sand and water for a funnel.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.help: Pour oil and water in a funnel and open the tap: the water comes first. Try sand and water and see that it is not suited.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.feedback: A separating funnel is for two liquids that do not mix, such as oil and water. The lower liquid is let out through the tap.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_METHO.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.error: Thinks filtering removes dissolved salt or sugar from water.

example.question: Salty water is poured through filter paper. What is in the water that comes through?
example.wrong_answer: Only water, the filter keeps the salt back
example.correct_answer: Water and the dissolved salt

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.cause: The child thinks the paper catches everything that is not water.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.reveals: Ask what drips through filter paper after salt solution and offer "only water".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.help: Filter salty water and taste it. It is still salty. Boil it down to see the salt.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.feedback: Dissolved salt is in tiny pieces that pass through the paper with the water. Filtering only keeps back bits too big to pass through, such as soil.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.source: Prieto, Blanco and Rodriguez (1989), International Journal of Science Education; Longden, Black and Solomon (1991), International Journal of Science Education (children on dissolving). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.error: Thinks that in winnowing the wind blows the heavy grain away and the light chaff stays.

example.question: When grain is winnowed, what does the wind blow away?
example.wrong_answer: The heavier grain
example.correct_answer: The lighter chaff

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.cause: The child has seen the activity but not tied the result to weight.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.reveals: Ask what the wind blows away and offer the grain.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.help: Drop a coin and a feather in front of a fan to see which one is blown away.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.feedback: The wind blows away the lighter chaff. The heavier grain falls straight down into the basin.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.error: Thinks the small pieces stay on the sieve and the big ones fall through.

example.question: Maize flour with husks is passed through a sieve. What stays on the sieve?
example.wrong_answer: The fine flour
example.correct_answer: The big husks

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.cause: The child thinks of the sieve as a net that catches little things.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.reveals: Ask what stays in the sieve and offer the fine flour.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.help: Sieve sand and small stones and look at what remains.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.feedback: The holes of a sieve let small pieces fall through. Pieces too big for the holes stay on top.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_PRINC.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..error: Thinks separating mixtures is only done in a science laboratory.

example.question: Where do people separate mixtures?
example.wrong_answer: Only in a science laboratory
example.correct_answer: At home, in the shamba and at work as well as in a laboratory

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..cause: The child connects science words with the lab.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..reveals: Ask where mixtures are separated and offer "only in a laboratory".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..help: List the actions a family does in a day: sieve flour, pick stones from beans, strain tea.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..feedback: People separate mixtures every day: sieving flour, picking stones from beans, straining tea, winnowing grain.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..error: Thinks filtering muddy water makes it safe to drink.

example.question: Muddy water is filtered through a clean cloth. Is the water now safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it looks clean
example.correct_answer: No, germs and dissolved things can still be in it

SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..cause: The child thinks that clear means safe.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..reveals: Ask whether filtered water is safe and offer "yes".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..help: Remember: germs are too small to be caught by a cloth. The water must also be boiled or treated.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..feedback: Filtering takes out the bits you can see, but germs and dissolved things are still there. The water must also be boiled or treated.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.MIXTURES.SEPARATION_USES..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.error: Thinks water is polluted only if dirt can be seen, so clear water is clean.

example.question: The water in a stream looks clear. Does that mean it is not polluted?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, clear water cannot be polluted
example.correct_answer: No, germs and chemicals cannot be seen

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.cause: The child uses looks as the test for clean water.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.reveals: Offer "clear water is clean" as an answer.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.help: Dissolve soap or salt in a glass of water: it is clear but not clean to drink.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.feedback: Germs and many chemicals cannot be seen. Clear water can still be polluted.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

example.question: Which of these can pollute a river?
example.wrong_answer: Only a factory pipe
example.correct_answer: A factory pipe, washing at the river and a latrine near the bank

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.cause: The child links pollution with big machines and smoke.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.reveals: Offer "only factories" and list home sources.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.help: Make a map of the school stream and list every source of waste along it.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.feedback: Homes, shambas and schools pollute water too: soap, rubbish, dung, fertiliser and latrines near the water.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.error: Thinks useful things such as soap and fertiliser cannot pollute water.

example.question: Fertiliser helps maize grow. Can it pollute a river?
example.wrong_answer: No, it helps plants so it cannot harm water
example.correct_answer: Yes, rain can wash it into the river and it harms living things there

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.cause: The child links useful with harmless.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.reveals: Use fertiliser, soap or pesticide and offer "cannot pollute".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.help: Look at a pond green with algae after too much fertiliser washed into it.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.feedback: Useful things pollute water when they get into it in the wrong place. Fertiliser and soap washed into a river harm the living things there.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTANT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks polluted water harms only people, not animals and plants.

example.question: Oil spills into a river. What happens to the fish?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, pollution only harms people
example.correct_answer: Many fish may die or fall ill

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child thinks of dirty water as a danger to drinkers.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.reveals: Ask about fish or crops and offer "nothing".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Look at pictures of an oil spill near a shore.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: Pollution harms plants and animals as well as people. Fish can die when the water is polluted.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks pollution harms only the place where it was dumped, not people downstream.

example.question: A factory dumps waste into a river. Who may be harmed?
example.wrong_answer: Only people next to the factory
example.correct_answer: People and animals living further down the river

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child pictures pollution as staying put.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.reveals: Ask who is harmed and offer "only the place where it was dumped".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Put food colouring in a gutter model and watch it travel.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: A river carries pollution with the water. People and animals far downstream can be harmed.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks polluted water is only a problem if it smells or tastes bad.

example.question: Water from a stream has no smell and no bad taste. Is it safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, it has no smell or taste
example.correct_answer: Not necessarily, it can have germs that cause diarrhoea

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child uses smell and taste as the test.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Remember that cholera germs have no smell.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: Germs have no taste or smell. Water can look and taste fine and still make you ill.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks a big river washes waste away, so a little rubbish does not matter.

example.question: Kamau says "The river is big, so one bag of rubbish does no harm." What is wrong with this?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, a big river washes it away
example.correct_answer: The waste does not disappear; it spreads and harms people and animals downstream

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child thinks that carrying away is the same as making harmless.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.reveals: Offer "the river is big" as an answer.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Show a bucket of coloured water poured into a larger bucket: the colour only spreads.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: A river does not make waste disappear. It carries it away to other places, where it still harms.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks a latrine close to a well or river is fine.

example.question: Where is the best place to dig a latrine?
example.wrong_answer: Next to the well, so it is easy to reach
example.correct_answer: Far from the well and the river

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child thinks of convenience, not of how water moves through the soil.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.reveals: Offer a place close to the water.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Pour coloured water through soil near a model well.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: Waste from a latrine can seep through the soil into wells and rivers. It must be dug far from them.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.error: Thinks washing clothes or cars in the river is harmless.

example.question: Where should a family wash clothes to keep a stream clean?
example.wrong_answer: In the stream, because the soap washes away
example.correct_answer: Away from the stream, pouring the used water on the ground

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.cause: The child sees the river as the easiest place for the job.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.help: Ask what is in used wash water: soap, oil and dirt.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.feedback: Soap and dirt harm fish and make the water unsafe for others. Wash at home and pour the used water on the ground.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.POLLUTION.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.error: Thinks filtering water makes it safe to drink.

example.question: A family filters stream water through cloth. What must they still do before drinking it?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, filtering makes it safe
example.correct_answer: Boil it or treat it to kill germs

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.cause: The child thinks that clear means safe and that filters kill germs.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.reveals: Ask what to do after filtering and offer "nothing".
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.help: Compare the water under a microscope picture: germs are far smaller than the holes in cloth.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.feedback: Filtering removes bits you can see. It does not kill germs. The water must be boiled or treated as well.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.error: Thinks boiling removes dirt and chemicals from water.

example.question: Water polluted with soap and oil is boiled. Is it now safe to drink?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, boiling removes everything harmful
example.correct_answer: No, boiling kills germs but does not remove soap or oil

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.cause: The child sees boiling as the cure for all water problems.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.reveals: Offer boiling for a chemical problem.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.help: Boil salty water: it is still salty.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.feedback: Boiling kills germs. It does not take out chemicals, soap or oil.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.error: Thinks muddy water can be treated in the sun in a bucket without filtering.

example.question: Which water is suitable for solar treatment in a clear plastic bottle?
example.wrong_answer: Muddy water straight from the river
example.correct_answer: Water that has been left to settle and filtered until it is clear

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.cause: The child does not know that mud blocks the sun's rays and shields germs.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.reveals: Offer muddy water for solar treatment.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.help: Place two bottles in the sun: one clear and one muddy.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.feedback: Sunlight must reach the germs. Muddy water blocks the light, so it must be settled and filtered first.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.source: Solar disinfection guidance (SODIS) commonly requires clear water. To confirm by a teacher.

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.error: Thinks more chlorine makes the water safer.

example.question: A mother adds three times the amount of water treatment tablet shown on the packet. What is the problem?
example.wrong_answer: None, more chlorine makes it safer
example.correct_answer: Too much chlorine makes the water taste bad and can harm people; the packet amount should be used

SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.cause: The child believes more of a cleaning thing is always better.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.feedback: Use exactly the amount on the packet. Too much chlorine gives a bad taste and can make you ill.
SCIE.G5.MATTER.WATER_POLLUTION.WATER_TRE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks heavy things sink and light things float.

example.question: A big wooden log is much heavier than a small stone. Which one sinks?
example.wrong_answer: The log, because it is heavier
example.correct_answer: The stone, even though it is lighter

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child uses weight alone, the quality that is easy to feel in the hand.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Pair a heavy floater (log) with a light sinker (small stone or nail).
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Drop a big log and a small stone in water. Repeat with a coin and a leaf.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: Weight alone does not decide. A heavy log floats and a small stone sinks. What matters is how heavy the object is for its size.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: Kohn (1993), Preschoolers' reasoning about density: will it float?, Child Development; Hsin and Wu (2011), Journal of Science Education and Technology; Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks a material always floats or always sinks: all metal sinks, all wood floats.

example.question: A steel ship is made of metal. Does it float or sink?
example.wrong_answer: It sinks, because all metal sinks
example.correct_answer: It floats

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child has learned a rule from a few objects and applies it to every object of that material.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Use a metal that floats (a tin bowl, a ship) or a wood that sinks (ebony).
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Float a tin lid on its flat side, then push it under so it fills with water.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: The material alone does not decide. A metal ship floats because of its shape, and a piece of ebony wood sinks. Test each object.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks an object that sinks in a basin would float in a lake because there is more water.

example.question: A stone sinks in a bucket of water. What happens if it is dropped in a deep lake?
example.wrong_answer: It floats, because the lake is deeper
example.correct_answer: It sinks, the same as in the bucket

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child thinks that more water holds things up more.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Drop the stone in a shallow dish and in a bucket. The result is the same.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: The amount of water does not change the result. A stone that sinks in a bucket sinks in a lake.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: Hsin and Wu (2011) report children citing the depth of water. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks shape makes no difference: a ball of clay sinks, so a bowl of the same clay sinks too.

example.question: A ball of clay sinks. The same clay is made into a bowl shape. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: It still sinks, because it is the same clay
example.correct_answer: It can float, because the bowl shape pushes aside more water

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child thinks of the material and mass only.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Use a same-material pair with two shapes and offer "no change".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Float a foil boat and then crumple the same foil into a ball.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: The same clay can float or sink depending on its shape. A bowl pushes aside more water, so it can float.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks only weight decides, so a heavier object always sinks.

example.question: Two blocks have the same size. Block A is heavier than block B. Which is more likely to sink?
example.wrong_answer: Both float the same way
example.correct_answer: Block A, which is heavier for its size

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child ignores size when it is the same, or ignores weight when it is not.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Use a same-size pair and offer "same result".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Compare two cups of the same size filled with sand and with cotton.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: For objects of the same size, the heavier one is more likely to sink. Weight and size must be thought about together.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: Kohn (1993); Hsin and Wu (2011). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks bigger pieces of the same material sink and smaller ones float (or the other way round).

example.question: A small piece of dry wood floats. Will a much bigger piece of the same wood float?
example.wrong_answer: No, it is too big
example.correct_answer: Yes, it floats too

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Compare big and small pieces of one material.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Float a splinter and a log of the same wood.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: Size alone does not decide. Big and small pieces of the same wood both float, because the wood is light for its size.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks adding a load to a floating object makes no difference.

example.question: More and more people climb into a small canoe on Lake Victoria. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing changes, it floats just as high
example.correct_answer: It floats lower and lower and can sink

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child has no idea of the push of water having a limit.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Use a canoe or a boat with passengers.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Add stones one by one to a floating plastic tub and watch it sink lower.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: Each added load makes the boat float lower. With too much load water comes over the side and it sinks.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.error: Thinks a steel ship floats because steel is lighter than water.

example.question: Why does a huge steel ship float?
example.wrong_answer: Because steel is lighter than water
example.correct_answer: Because its shape pushes aside a lot of water

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child thinks floating means the material is light.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Ask why the ship floats and offer "steel is light".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: A steel nail sinks. Shape the same steel into a bowl and it floats.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: Steel is heavier than water. A ship floats because it is shaped like a big hollow bowl that pushes aside a lot of water.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

example.question: A floating log is lifted out of the water onto a scale. What does the scale show?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing, because floating things have no weight
example.correct_answer: Its weight, as the log is heavy

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.cause: The child thinks "not sinking" means "not heavy".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.reveals: Ask about the weight of a floating thing.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.help: Weigh a block of wood that floats.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.feedback: A floating object still has weight. It floats because the water pushes it up.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.FLOATING_AND_SINKING.FLOA.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.error: Thinks sound is made without anything moving, or that the sound is "in" the object.

example.question: What happens to the skin of a drum when it makes a sound?
example.wrong_answer: It stays still; the sound is inside the drum
example.correct_answer: It vibrates, moving quickly to and fro

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.cause: The child cannot see the vibration and thinks nothing moves.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.reveals: Ask what the drum skin does and offer "stays still".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.help: Put rice grains on a drum and hit it: they jump. Hold a ruler off the edge of a desk and twang it.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.feedback: Every sound is made by something vibrating. The drum skin moves quickly to and fro, and the rice on it jumps.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006), Sound stuff? Naive materialism in middle-school students' conceptions of sound, International Journal of Science Education. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.error: Thinks that in a flute or whistle the air is not part of the sound, only the instrument.

example.question: What vibrates to make the sound in a flute?
example.wrong_answer: The metal or wood of the flute only
example.correct_answer: The air inside the flute

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.cause: The child sees the instrument as the object that moves.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.reveals: Ask what vibrates in a flute and offer the flute itself.
