SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.help: Blow across the top of a bottle and change the water level.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.feedback: In a flute or whistle the air inside the pipe vibrates. The vibrating air makes the sound.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.error: Thinks sound is only made by hitting or banging things.

example.question: Which action can make a sound from a string?
example.wrong_answer: Only hitting it with a stick
example.correct_answer: Plucking it with a finger

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.cause: The child has met drums and bells mostly.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.reveals: Offer hitting as the only way.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.help: Pluck a stretched rubber band, then blow across a bottle: sound without banging.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.feedback: Sound can come from plucking, blowing, rubbing or banging. What matters is that something vibrates.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_SOURCE.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.error: Thinks sound travels only through air, not through water or solids.

example.question: A learner puts an ear to a wooden desk while a friend taps the other end. What happens?
example.wrong_answer: She hears nothing, because sound only travels through air
example.correct_answer: She hears the tap clearly, because sound travels through the wood

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.cause: The child associates sound with the air they live in.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.reveals: Use a solid or water and offer "only air".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.help: Tap a desk and listen with the ear on it. Swimmers hear sounds under water.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.feedback: Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. It can even go through wood and water.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006); Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

example.question: An astronaut outside a spacecraft shouts. Can another astronaut far away hear it?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, sound travels everywhere
example.correct_answer: No, there is no air or other material in space to carry the sound

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.cause: Films show explosions in space with sound.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.reveals: Ask whether space can carry sound and offer "yes".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.help: Ring a bell in a jar with the air pumped out (video). It goes quiet.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.feedback: Sound needs something to travel through, such as air, water or a solid. Space is empty, so sound cannot travel there.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.error: Thinks sound travels faster through air than through solids or water.

example.question: Through which material does sound travel fastest?
example.wrong_answer: Air
example.correct_answer: Steel

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.cause: The child thinks that lighter materials let things travel faster.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.help: Listen to a train through a rail and through the air.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.feedback: Sound travels fastest through solids such as steel, slower through water and slowest through air.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.source: Eshach and Schwartz (2006) report this reversal. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.error: Thinks a louder sound travels faster than a quiet one.

example.question: Two drums are played, one very loud and one very quiet, at the same distance. Which sound arrives first?
example.wrong_answer: The louder one
example.correct_answer: They arrive at the same time

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.cause: The child links loud with strong and strong with quick.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.help: Watch a band at a distance: loud and quiet notes of the same beat arrive together.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.feedback: Loudness does not change speed. The sound from a loud drum and a quiet drum take the same time to arrive.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_TRAVEL.source: Wittmann, Steinberg and Redish (1999) on students' ideas about wave speed. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.error: Thinks loud sound affects only the ears, and only for a short time.

example.question: Which problems can very loud noise cause?
example.wrong_answer: It only makes the ears ring for a moment
example.correct_answer: Damage to hearing, headaches and poor sleep

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.cause: The child has felt ringing ears after a loud noise and thinks that is all.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.reveals: Ask what loud noise can cause and offer the short ringing.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.help: Ask the class how they feel after a long day in a very noisy place.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.feedback: Very loud sound can damage hearing for good. It can also cause headaches, stress and poor sleep.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.error: Thinks that being used to a loud noise means it no longer harms.

example.question: A boda boda rider has driven near loud engines for years and says he is now used to the noise. What is true?
example.wrong_answer: Because he is used to it, the noise cannot harm his hearing
example.correct_answer: His hearing can still be getting damaged even if the noise no longer bothers him

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.cause: The child thinks that feeling no discomfort means no harm.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.reveals: Offer "used to it, so no harm".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.help: Explain that the tiny hair cells in the ear are not renewed once damaged.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.feedback: Feeling used to a noise does not stop the damage. Loud noise can still harm hearing, so ear protection is needed.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.error: Thinks loud music cannot harm hearing because it is pleasant.

example.question: A matatu plays music at full volume every day. What is true for the passengers?
example.wrong_answer: It cannot harm them, because music is pleasant
example.correct_answer: It can harm their hearing, because any very loud sound can

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.cause: The child thinks that "noise" means only unpleasant sounds.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.help: Ask what happens to the ears at a very loud concert.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.feedback: It is the loudness, not the kind of sound, that harms. Very loud music can damage hearing as well.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.SOUND_ENERGY.SOUND_EFFECT.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..error: Thinks heat itself rises, so heat can only go upwards.

example.question: A hot metal rod is held sideways. In which direction does the heat spread?
example.wrong_answer: Only upwards, because heat rises
example.correct_answer: Along the rod, away from the hot end, in every direction

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..cause: The child has heard "heat rises" and turns it into a rule about all heat.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..reveals: Use a sideways or downward situation and offer "up only".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..help: Hold a lit candle under, beside and over your hand and feel the warmth in all of them.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..feedback: Hot air rises, but heat is not limited to going up. In a solid, heat spreads along it from the hot end to the colder parts.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge; Erickson (1979), Children's conceptions of heat and temperature, Science Education. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..error: Thinks cold flows from ice or a cold object into a warm one.

example.question: A cold drink is held in a warm hand. What is moving?
example.wrong_answer: Cold moves from the drink into the hand
example.correct_answer: Heat moves from the hand into the drink

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..cause: The child feels the cold and thinks something cold is arriving.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..help: Put a thermometer in the hand and then on the bottle.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..feedback: There is no flow of cold. Heat always moves from a warmer thing to a colder thing, so the hand loses heat to the drink.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..source: Erickson (1979); Wiser and Carey (1983). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..error: Thinks the sun's heat reaches us by conduction through air, or needs air to travel.

example.question: Space between the Sun and the Earth is empty. How does the Sun's heat reach us?
example.wrong_answer: By conduction through the air
example.correct_answer: By radiation, which needs nothing to carry it

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..cause: The child pictures heat as needing something to travel through, like sound.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..reveals: Ask how the sun's heat arrives and offer conduction.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..help: Hold a hand near a lit lamp and feel the warmth without touching.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..feedback: Radiation is heat that travels without anything to carry it. That is how the Sun's heat crosses empty space.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..error: Thinks convection can happen in solids, such as along a metal spoon.

example.question: Which mode moves heat along a metal spoon placed in hot tea?
example.wrong_answer: Convection
example.correct_answer: Conduction

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..cause: The child has memorised the names and cannot tell which fits which material.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..help: Convection needs a fluid that can move. A spoon cannot move its particles around.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..feedback: Convection happens only in liquids and gases that can flow. Heat moves along a solid by conduction.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_MODES..source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.error: Thinks metal is colder than wood or plastic because it feels colder.

example.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room all night. Which one is colder?
example.wrong_answer: The metal spoon, because it feels colder
example.correct_answer: Neither, they are the same temperature

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.cause: The child uses the feeling in the hand as the temperature.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.reveals: Use two things left in the same room and offer "metal is colder".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.help: Measure both with a thermometer: the reading is the same.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.feedback: Both are at the temperature of the room. Metal feels colder because it takes heat away from your hand faster.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.source: Erickson (1979); Wiser and Carey (1983); Harrison, Grayson and Treagust (1999). Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.error: Thinks wool and blankets make heat of their own.

example.question: A cold child is wrapped in a woollen blanket. Where does the warmth come from?
example.wrong_answer: The blanket makes heat
example.correct_answer: The child's own body, kept in by the blanket

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.cause: The child feels warmth and credits the thing wrapped around.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.reveals: Put a thermometer in a blanket alone and offer "the blanket makes heat".
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.help: Wrap a thermometer in a blanket: the temperature does not rise. Wrap a warm bottle and watch it stay warm.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.feedback: A blanket is a poor conductor. It keeps your own heat in, but it makes no heat. A blanket around a thermometer does not make it warmer.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.source: Driver, Squires, Rushworth and Wood-Robinson (1994), Making Sense of Secondary Science, Routledge. Cited from memory.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.error: Thinks a good conductor of heat keeps heat in for a long time.

example.question: Which pot handle is better for a hot sufuria?
example.wrong_answer: Metal, because metal holds heat in
example.correct_answer: Wood, because it does not carry heat to the hand

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.cause: The child mixes up carrying heat (conducting) with keeping heat in.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.reveals: Ask which handle is safe and offer metal.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.help: Put a metal and a wooden spoon in hot water and feel the handles after a minute.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.feedback: A good conductor carries heat quickly, so a metal handle gets hot too. A poor conductor such as wood keeps the heat from your hand.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_CONDUC.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.error: Thinks the colour of a surface makes no difference to how hot it gets in the sun.

example.question: Two iron sheet roofs, one painted white and one painted black, stand in the sun. Which gets hotter?
example.wrong_answer: Both the same, colour makes no difference
example.correct_answer: The black one, as dark surfaces take in more of the sun's heat

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.cause: The child has not compared surfaces in the sun.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.help: Put a white and a black tin in the sun with thermometers.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.feedback: Dark surfaces take in more of the sun's radiation and get hotter. Light surfaces reflect more and stay cooler.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.error: Thinks air vents for a hot room or kitchen are best low on the wall, because heat goes down.

example.question: Why is a vent put near the roof of a hot kitchen?
example.wrong_answer: Heat goes downwards, so the vent has to catch it
example.correct_answer: Hot air and smoke rise, so they go out through the vent at the top

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.cause: The child has not met convection in air.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.reveals: Offer a vent near the floor as correct.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.help: Hold a candle flame near the top and bottom of a doorway and see the smoke go.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.feedback: Hot air is lighter and rises, so smoke and hot air can leave through a high vent. This is convection.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.error: Thinks heat transfer matters only when cooking.

example.question: Which of these uses heat transfer?
example.wrong_answer: Only cooking uses it
example.correct_answer: Cooking, drying clothes in the sun and a flask that keeps tea hot all use it

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.cause: The child thinks of heat in the kitchen only.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.help: List the places in a day where heat moves: sun on the roof, tea cooling, wearing a jumper.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.feedback: Heat moves everywhere: when we cook, dry clothes in the sun and keep tea hot in a flask.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_USES.M.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.error: Thinks a wet cloth is the safest thing to hold a hot sufuria with.

example.question: Wanjiru needs to lift a hot sufuria. Which cloth is safest to use?
example.wrong_answer: A wet cloth, because water cools it
example.correct_answer: A dry, thick cloth

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.cause: The child thinks water always cools things.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.help: A wet cloth conducts heat and steam burns. Compare a dry and a wet cloth on a warm tin.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.feedback: A wet cloth conducts heat to your hand and makes steam, which burns. Use a thick dry cloth.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.error: Thinks a pot that is no longer on the fire, or has no flame or steam, is safe to touch.

example.question: A sufuria has just been taken off the jiko. There is no flame or steam. Is it safe to touch?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, there is no flame or steam so it is cool
example.correct_answer: No, it can stay hot for a long time

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.cause: The child uses flame or steam as the sign of heat.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.help: Hold a hand near, not on, the pot and feel the heat.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.feedback: Metal can stay very hot for a long time even when there is no flame or steam. Do not touch it.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.error: Thinks a metal handle on a hot pan is safe because metal is strong.

example.question: A sufuria has a metal handle. What is the danger when it is on the fire?
example.wrong_answer: None, metal is strong and safe
example.correct_answer: The handle gets hot because metal carries heat to it

SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.cause: The child mixes up strong with safe.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.help: Put a metal and a wooden spoon in hot water and feel both handles.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.feedback: Metal is a good conductor, so the handle becomes hot too. Always use a dry cloth to hold a metal handle.
SCIE.G5.FORCE_.HEAT_TRANSFER.HEAT_SAFETY.source: To confirm by a teacher: common in classrooms, not traced to a study by the author.
